questions.question: What motivated you to go on exchange? (pick the most important one) *
questions.answer: Academic opportunities

questions.question: Which aspects were crucial to choosing your study destination? *
questions.answer: I had both academic and personal reasons for going on exchange. Academically I thought it would give me the opportunity to be taught in a different way than I'm used to, furthering my academic experience and abilities. Personally, exchange is a wonderful way to get out of your comfort zone and meet a bunch of new people from all over the world.

questions.question: How would you rate your overall study abroad experience? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer: I had a really good experience both academically and personally, although balancing both having a full-time study, finding yourself in a new country/city, and finding new friends, was a challenge. Definitely worth it though!

questions.question: How easy was it to find the information you needed to know upon arrival? *
questions.answer: VU Amsterdam was very good at providing relatively timely information about almost everything. And if you still lack information on something they were really quick to respond per mail.

questions.question: What assistance, if any, did you receive when you arrived at your study destination? *
questions.answer: VU had some tutors we could ask questions during most of the intro days. We did have to do a self-guided tour around campus, which felt kind of pointless. Especially since it was self-guided.

questions.question: Overall, how satisfied were you with the orientation and assistance available to students at your host institution upon arrival? *
Additional comments
questions.answer: We had a two week introduction period where we had a bunch of events offered to us, both academically and socially oriented. Most of the things were really fun, and it was a good way of having something to do the first couple of weeks after your arrival, and a wonderful way of getting to meet a bunch of really great people. I made a bunch of friends during these weeks.

questions.question: How did you find housing? *
questions.answer: I found housing through my host institution

questions.question: Did you live on campus or off campus? *
questions.answer: Off campus

questions.question: How easy was it to find off campus housing? Any recommendations? *
questions.answer:
Amsterdam has a crazy housing crisis, so finding housing is pretty hard. Especially because there are so many people fighting to get the same apartments, rooms, etc. We got access to a website called Rooms, where different accommodation options were listed, and you definitely have to prepare yourself and be ready to reserve the room/apartment you want when they open access to booking. I had a friend who went to book a room weeks after everyone had booked through Rooms, and he ended up having to live on a camping site because there was no where else for him to live.
I had booked a room on campus through Rooms, which turned out to be double booked, and VU was not super helpful about it. So I ended up renting a private apartment off campus that was way, way, way over my budget and I went from thinking I was going to pay 400-ish euros to 1500 euros a month... pretty rough.
I would however still recommend signing up for housing through uni for sure (though I have friends who managed to figure it out themselves), because the chances of finding something through various internet/FB sites are small, and you run the risk of getting ripped off and not having anywhere to stay, since you can't check and see the apartment before arriving. So it's all around safer through uni.

questions.question: What should future exchange students know about living off campus? *
questions.answer: Be aware that if you are renting privately instead of through a company on campus, the renting period might be different. The beautiful (but very expensive) apartment I rented was from a girl who herself was going on exchange. But since her exchange period was shorter than mine, I had to find somewhere else to live in the last month of exchange because she came back to Amsterdam and naturally had to live in her own apartment. Renting accommodation on campus is usually fitted to the semester at uni, so you should be able to stay there throughout the whole semester.

questions.question: Overall, how satisfied were you with the housing available to students? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer: If you're not living on campus, make friends with people who are, because there are a lot of really fun parties there, and having friends who have more communal living makes it really easy to expand your social circle.

questions.question: How easy did you find the registration process at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer: VU made pretty well-structured guides on what information they needed and when.

questions.question: Please describe the registration process at your host institution *
questions.answer: VU sent various links to forms we had to fill in regarding which semester you were registering for, what kind of exchange student you were (semester/full year), passport information etc.

questions.question: What kind of help was available? *
questions.answer: They answer relatively fast per email!

questions.question: How successful were you in registering for the classes you wanted? *
questions.answer: I got to register for all the classes I wanted. They did however have to change one of the courses in the minor to another, that they registered me for instead, which was fine with me as it fitted pretty well into what the minor was about (Gender and Diversity)

questions.question: What advice would you offer to future exchange students about registration at your host institution? *
questions.answer: Don't hesitate to send a bunch of emails, even if you think they are dumb questions. Also, talk with your friends if you know people who are going to the same place as you. It helped me a lot to do the more important forms etc. with someone.

questions.question: How satisfied were you with the academic programme at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
Were you a BA or MA student at UCPH when you were on exchange? *
questions.answer: BA

questions.question: Please elaborate on the level of courses *
questions.answer: I took 30 ECTS as electives, and I chose a minor programme called 'Gender and Diversity'. I took 5 courses (6ECTS each) all but one, were 300 points/level and the last one was 200.

questions.question: How did the style of teaching at your host institution compare with that of UCPH? *
questions.answer: The semester was from the beginning of September till the end of January/beginning of February depending on exams. At VU they split the semester up into three periods: P1 = 2 months; P2 = 2 months; P3 = 1 month, and typically you will have two courses in each P1 and P2 and one course in P3

questions.question: How long were you on exchange? *
questions.answer: 1 semester

questions.question: Please list the courses you were enrolled in during your first semester. *
questions.answer: Identity, Diversity and Inclusion; Religions and Gender; Sexual Health: Threats and Opportunities for minor GAD; Theorizing Gender and Intersectionality; Diversifying Philosophy

questions.question: What specific courses would you recommend to future exchange students? Why? *
questions.answer:
Identity, Diversity and Inclusion was a really cool course! The professors were super nice and very good at engaging the students. The contents of the course were also incredibly interesting - The course focused in particular on contemporary issues concerning processes of inclusion and exclusion in the Dutch/European context.
The central questions in this course were:
1. How and why are identities based on ethnicity, gender, class and sexuality constructed by both insiders and outsiders?
2. How do (groups within) European/Dutch societies respond to diversity? 3. What are the relevant mechanisms of inclusion or exclusion?
4. How should we contextualize current debates and practices related to inclusion/exclusion processes in relation to Dutch/European historical developments?

What unexpected costs did you encounter? *
questions.answer: If you live in private housing as I did, they have taxes on trash, which is pretty expensive!! I had to pay around 100 Euros from august til January, and it is really difficult because you have to have a dutch bank account. and do it through their municipality website with a special login (similar to MitID/NemID), which. took a while to sort out.

questions.question: What items were more or less expensive than you expected? *
questions.answer: I feel like it is pretty much the same as in DK

questions.question: How satisfied were you with the non-academic opportunities (clubs, sports, etc.) at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
What kinds of cultural, athletic and social activities were available for students at your host institution? *
questions.answer: During the introduction period, they had classes you could sign up with, like yoga, football/soccer, various dance classes etc. Most of these classes were also available after the introduction period through memberships.

questions.question: Which non -academic activities would you recommend to future exchange students? Why? *
questions.answer: Explore the city! Amsterdam is BEAUTIFUL, and it has so many attractions to visit. If you plan to visit more than 4 of the big museums, I would recommend buying a 'museum card'. It is super worth it for the price and you get access to A LOT of museums all over The Netherlands.

questions.question: What do you recommend other visiting students see or do on their weekends or holidays? *
questions.answer: Museums, visiting other cities (Den Haag, Utrecht, Rotterdam, Delft...), just walking around enjoying the city!!

questions.question: How easy was it to adjust to the local culture of your exchange site? *
questions.answer: Easy. I feel Dutch people a very similar to Danes.

questions.question: Do you have any tips for socializing with local students?
questions.answer: Some say they can be quite direct, which can come as a shock to people, so this is maybe something to be aware of. I didn't find them overly direct though.

questions.question: What, if any, cultural differences did you find particularly challenging? *
questions.answer: Don't have any

questions.question: What parts of the culture did you most appreciate? *
questions.answer: The architecture

questions.question: What are the three most important things you would tell a UCPH student who is going to your host institution on exchange? *
questions.answer:
1) Read the course manuals very well
2) BE PREPARED FOR THE HOUSING SITUATION
3) Join as many introduction events as possible - even though it is overwhelming in the beginning, it pays off socially in the end

questions.question: Is there any other information that you think might prove useful to future exchange students attending your host institution? *
questions.answer: Nope

questions.question: What was the most rewarding part of your exchange experience? *
questions.answer: The friends I have made <3

questions.question: What was the greatest challenge during the exchange? *
questions.answer: Balancing both wanting to have fun, travel, explore, party etc. and having a full-time study.

questions.question: Any other comments?
Do you agree to share your travel report with other fellow students? *
questions.answer: Yes
